title: var vs :=, zero values, constants and iota
summary: Every Go variable starts at a usable zero value, := declares while = assigns, and constants are exact compile-time values that iota can enumerate.

examples.title: Zero values are usable, not just empty

annotations.note: There is no "uninitialized" state: var gives every field its zero value ("", 0, false, nil). Unlike C, no garbage; unlike Java, a string field is "" rather than null.
A nil slice is a valid empty slice (append allocates on demand) and a nil map reads as empty. Only writing to a nil map panics, as the comment on the next line says.
:= declares and infers the type, inside functions only. With several names on the left it needs at least one new one; the others are plainly assigned, which is how n changes from 3 to 4 here.
Both right-hand values are read before either variable is written, so a swap needs no temporary.

examples.title: The := shadowing bug and its one-character fix

annotations.note: Inside the block, := declares brand-new result and err that hide the outer ones. The outer variables are never written, and it compiles because the inner ones are used. Default go vet doesn't report it.
= assigns the variables declared on lines 16-17. When a block should update outer state, declare first and assign inside.

examples.title: Typed enums with iota, and untyped constants

annotations.note: iota is the line index inside one const block, starting at 0. A line without an expression repeats the previous one, type included, so all four constants are Level values.
A String method makes Level a fmt.Stringer, so fmt prints names. The fallback keeps an unknown value like Level(7) debuggable.
The blank identifier skips iota's 0; the repeated expression then yields 1<<10, 1<<20 and 1<<30.
Untyped constants are exact values of arbitrary precision. 1<<100 never exists at run time; only the result 4 has to fit in an int.
The untyped 2 takes its type from time.Second, a time.Duration. The same with a variable n would need time.Duration(n): the next lesson.

use_cases: var x T when the zero value is what you want, or a declaration without an obvious initial value
:= for nearly every local variable, especially results of calls: v, err := f()
const + iota for enum-like sets (log levels, states) with a String method
Untyped constants for unit math such as KB/MB or timeouts (2 * time.Second)
strengths: Zero values remove a whole class of null checks: a zero sync.Mutex, bytes.Buffer or empty struct is ready to use, unlike Java fields that start as null
Constants are checked at compile time with exact arithmetic, so 1<<100 overflow mistakes surface as compile errors rather than wrapped values at run time
Declaration forms are few: var, :=, const. No let/var/const scoping puzzles as in pre-ES6 JavaScript
weaknesses: iota enums are just integers: any int converts to Level, and nothing checks a switch for exhaustiveness the way TypeScript's never does
:= in an inner scope silently shadows outer variables, and the default go vet doesn't report it
A zero value isn't always meaningful: 0 retries or an empty name may be a real setting or a forgotten field, and the type can't tell you which

pitfalls.title: Shadowing err or a result inside if/for blocks
pitfalls.detail: x, err := f() inside a block creates new variables; the outer ones keep their old values. Declare outside and use = inside when the block should update them.

pitfalls.title: Writing to a nil map
pitfalls.detail: Reading a nil map is fine, writing panics. Initialize maps with make (or a literal) before the first write.

pitfalls.title: Relying on iota values in storage
pitfalls.detail: Inserting a new constant in the middle renumbers everything after it. Persist names (or explicit numbers), not iota positions.

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println print for a struct field `Tags []string` that was never assigned?
quiz.why: The field's zero value is a nil slice, and fmt prints a nil slice as [].

quiz.q: `a, err := f()` appears inside an if block while a and err are already declared outside. What happens?
options: The outer a and err are assigned
New a and err are declared for the block; the outer ones are untouched
quiz.why: The block is a new scope, so := declares fresh variables there. The 'no new variables' error only applies within the same scope.

quiz.q: In `const ( A = iota * 10; B; C )`, what is C?
quiz.why: B and C repeat the expression iota * 10 with iota = 1 and 2.

body:
## Concept

Go has three ways to introduce a name: `var x T` (zero value), `x := expr` (declare and
infer, inside functions only) and `const`. There is no uninitialized memory: every
variable starts at its type's zero value, and the standard library designs types so that
the zero value works (a zero `sync.Mutex` is unlocked, a zero `bytes.Buffer` is empty and
ready). Constants are compile-time values with exact arithmetic; `iota` numbers the lines
of a `const` block, which is how Go spells enums.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: no uninitialized locals and no constructors; `var c Config` is fully initialized.
- Java: no `null` for strings or numbers. Only pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions
  and interfaces have `nil` as their zero value.
- Python: names are declared, not created on first assignment, and a typo in an
  assignment is a compile error instead of a new variable.
- JS/TS: `:=` is roughly `let` with inference, but there is no `undefined`. A `const`
  in Go must be a compile-time value; JS `const` only forbids reassignment.
- Java/TS enums are their own types with a closed set of values. Go's `iota` constants
  are named integers: nothing stops `Level(7)`.

## Design notes

Prefer `:=` for locals and `var` when the zero value is the point (`var buf
bytes.Buffer`). Make your own types useful at their zero value where you can: then
callers never need a constructor for the common case. For enums, add a `String` method
and handle the unknown case explicitly, because the compiler won't check that a
`switch` covers every constant. Watch for `:=` inside `if`/`for` blocks whenever you mean
to update an outer variable; it is the most common beginner bug that compiles cleanly.

files.examples/01_zero_values.go:
package main

import "fmt"

type Config struct {
	Name    string
	Retries int
	Debug   bool
	Tags    []string
	Limits  map[string]int
}

func main() {
	var c Config // no constructor: every field starts at its zero value
	fmt.Printf("%q %d %t %v %v\n", c.Name, c.Retries, c.Debug, c.Tags, c.Limits)
	fmt.Println("nil slice:", c.Tags == nil, "nil map:", c.Limits == nil)

	// Zero values are usable, not just "empty":
	c.Tags = append(c.Tags, "beta")           // append allocates on demand
	fmt.Println(len(c.Limits), c.Limits["x"]) // reading a nil map is fine
	// c.Limits["x"] = 1 would panic: writing needs make(map[string]int)

	n := 3               // short declaration: infers int, function bodies only
	n, extra := 4, "new" // legal: extra is new, so n is only assigned
	a, b := 1, 2
	a, b = b, a // tuple assignment, no temp variable
	fmt.Println(c.Tags, n, extra, a, b)
}

expected.zero-values:
"" 0 false [] map[]
nil slice: true nil map: true
0 0
[beta] 4 new 2 1
expected.shadowing:
inner: value-of-a <nil>
outer after bug: "" <nil>
outer after fix: "value-of-b" <nil>
